Session Design
Session Summary: Democracy and Anticorruption - Responding to Backsliding and Opportunities
Session Owners: Peter Wiebler (Zambia); April Hahn (MENA), Luis Azurduy (LAC), Mark Billera (DRG), Meral Karan (DRG), Abigail Bellows (ACTF)
Session Objectives:
Date: Oct 25
Time: 3:30-4:50
(1) MDs are updated on important developments in Administration policy and Agency priorities.
(2) MDs will be more informed on currenttrends in democratic backsliding and how it affects USAID's entire portfolio.
(3) MDs will understand available tools, resources and approaches to support democratic resilience, and mitigate and adapt
programming in the face of democratic backsliding.
Overview/ Description: Provide a summary description of what you are trying to achieve and how you will do that in this session. This section of the template
is essential for conveying your approach to the Core Group. Consider the following points:
• Why is the session important for Mission Directors?
It's important that MDs understand the changing DRG landscape, including the impacts of transnational and geopolitical influences and how that
relates to the USAID portfolio, regardless of technical sector.
Agency attention and funding for DRG has increased. This session will help MDs understand Agency priorities and what to expect regarding
funding and programs.
• What are the main take-away points?
Democratic governance is critical for development and vice versa - they are mutually reinforcing. Mission Directors can play a critical role in
supporting DRG and cross-sectoral programs and goals, both in closing and opening political environments.
• Threats to democracy have changed and are impacting USAID in new ways. Identify the signs of democratic backsliding and the authoritarian
playbook to support a whole of mission approach to prevention and response.
DRG Resources and new approaches are coming to support Missions
• How will you engage MDs in the session?
Initial plenary with presentation (30 minutes) + Q&A (30 minutes)
•3 Small break out groups (Co facilitated by a Mission Director & USAID DRG Expert paired per small group)
•

• How will you focus on practical implementation?
o Share specific tools and approaches being developed to assist missions in addressing emerging DRG challenges

Explore engagement beyond DRG programming, e.g. Mission-wide approaches, in the interagency, and donor coordination.

Gather recommendations/requests from MDs for the upcoming Summit for Democracy
• Aretherecross-cutting issues that are important to highlight?
Many DRG issues are inherently cross cutting - we will make that point. Specific issues of anti-corruption, disinformation, foreign malign
influence and gender are cross-cutting and will be included.

Small Group C: Operating in Politically Dynamic Environments (Plenary Room)
This session will discuss common trajectories of closing political environments, impacts
on programming, staff and security, and strategies to support democratic resilience and
progress. Additionally, there are different US political considerations - some closing
political environments where we vigorously stand up for democracy (Belarus) anc
others where seek to engage with governments regardless of repressions
(Azerbaijan or Tajikistan). We will need to address both environments and what it
means for our DG work.
Co-Facilitator Laura Pavlovic, Deputy Director/DRG Center/DDI
Ryan Washburn, Mission Director
Chris Cushing, Mission Director, El Salvador
Questions to ask group:
1. What diplomatic efforts or strategies have you used to address democratic
backsliding or support democratic openings? What holds you back?
2. What are the trade offs, as a Mission Director, when working with counterparts
4

that are increasingly autocratic? Do you have best practices of working in the
inter-agency to ensure the USG speaks with one voice on democratic
backsliding?
3. What operational issues do you face in addressing these challenges and what
would help you manage them? (i.e. cybersecurity, IP/staff security, crisis
communications, etc)
4. Openings are crucial but they can close quickly. What should USAID do to
orepare for them and keep them open?

Shannon Green, Executive Director, Anticorruption Task Force
[contact omitted]
Shannon N. Green serves as Senior Advisor to the Administrator and Executive Director of the
Anti-Corruption Task Force. Previously, Ms. Green was the Senior Director of Programs at the Center for
Civilians in Conflict (CIVIC), where she oversaw the organization's global efforts to recognize the dignity
and rights of civilians, prevent civilian harm, and protect civilians caught in conflict. Before that, she was
the Director and Senior Fellow of the Human Rights Initiative at the Center for Strategic and International
Studies (CSIS), where her research focused on addressing threats to democratic institutions and norms;
enhancing justice and accountability; and improving security forces' respect for human rights.
Peter Wiebler
[contact omitted]
Peter Wiebler is the Mission Director of USAID/Zambia. Before his appointment to Zambia, Mr. Wiebler
served as Mission Director for USAID/Caucasus in Tbilisi, Georgia from 2018-2022. A career Senior
Foreign Service Officer, Mr. Wiebler has extensive senior U.S. Government and private foundation
experience in democratization. Prior to his assignment to Georgia, Mr. Wiebler served as the Acting
Director of the Office of Budget and Resource Management (BRM) in USAID/Washington and has led the
Democracy and Governance (DG) portfolios in some of the Agency's largest and most sensitive missions,
including Afghanistan, Belarus, Moldova, West Bank/Gaza, Serbia, and Ukraine. Prior to joining USAID in
2002, Mr. Wiebler led Freedom House's Budapest Regional Office for seven years, spearheading
democratization initiatives across Central and Eastern Europe.
Vera Zakem
[contact omitted]
Vera Zakem is Senior Advisor for Technology and Democracy, based in the DRG Center, leading USAID's
efforts to strengthen information integrity and digital democracy. She has served as a Senior Technology
and Policy Advisor atthe Institute for Security and Technology and led strategy and research at Twitter.

has more than 25 years of experience with USAID and the U.S. Department of State on a wide range of
democracy and governance, conflict mitigation and fragile states initiatives. Previously, Ms. Brown served
as Senior Advisor in the Bureau for Policy, Planning and Learning, visiting faculty at the National Defense
University's Eisenhower School, the acting Deputy Assistant Administrator in USAID's Bureau for
Democracy, Conflict, and Humanitarian Assistance, and the Director of USAID's Office of Conflict
Management and Mitigation. She joined USAID as a Presidential Management Intern, contributing to the
establishment of the Democracy and Governance Center of Excellence and also served at USAID/Nigeria.
